topics.name: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
topics.summary: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Spherical mirrors are handled with the Cartesian sign convention: every distance is measured from the pole, and the direction of the incident light is positive. Objects are placed on the left, so \( u \) is negative. A concave mirror has its focus in front, so its \( f \) is negative; a convex mirror has its focus behind, so its \( f \) is positive. The focal length is half the radius of curvature. The mirror formula adds reciprocals, and the magnification carries a minus sign. A negative magnification means an inverted (real) image; a positive one means an erect (virtual) image. A concave mirror gives real images for objects beyond the focus and a magnified virtual image for objects inside it, while a convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image, which is why it is used as a rear-view mirror. The mirror formula is not the lens formula: keep the two sign patterns separate.
topics.worked_example: An object is 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. With \( u=-20 \) cm and \( f=-15 \) cm, \( \dfrac{1}{v}=-\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{20}=-\dfrac{1}{60} \), so \( v=-60 \) cm. Then \( m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=-3 \): a real, inverted image three times the size, 60 cm in front of the mirror.
common_mistakes: Using the lens formula \( \dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \) or the lens magnification \( \dfrac{v}{u} \) for a mirror
Giving a concave mirror a positive focal length because a converging lens has one
Taking the focal length equal to the radius instead of half of it
Reading a negative magnification as a virtual image

topics.name: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
topics.summary: Refractive index is \( \mu=\dfrac{c}{v} \); since \( \mu\gt1 \) for any real medium, light always travels slower in the denser medium. Snell's law \( \mu_1\sin i=\mu_2\sin r \) says light bends toward the normal on entering a denser medium and away from it on entering a rarer one. An object under a liquid appears raised: apparent depth is real depth divided by \( \mu \). When light goes from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle \( C \), no light is refracted and total internal reflection occurs; here \( \sin C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \), with \( \mu \) the denser medium's index relative to the rarer one. TIR can never happen going from rarer to denser. It explains optical fibres, sparkling diamonds and reflecting prisms. At a single spherical surface separating two media, the image follows the single-surface formula, with \( R \) signed by where the centre of curvature lies. This relation is the building block of the lens maker's formula.
topics.worked_example: A medium has \( \mu=2 \). Its critical angle with air satisfies \( \sin C=\dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( C=30^\circ \). A ray inside this medium meeting the surface at \( 40^\circ \) is totally reflected, but a ray in air entering it at any angle simply refracts in.
common_mistakes: Writing \( C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \) instead of \( \sin C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \)
Allowing TIR for light going from a rarer into a denser medium
Claiming light speeds up in a denser medium
Multiplying the real depth by the refractive index instead of dividing

topics.name: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
topics.summary: A thin lens is described with distances measured from its optical centre and incident light positive. A convex (converging) lens has positive \( f \); a concave (diverging) lens has negative \( f \), the opposite of how the words concave and convex map onto mirror signs. The lens formula subtracts reciprocals, and the magnification has no minus sign. The lens maker's formula links \( f \) to the material and shapes; in a surrounding medium, \( \mu \) is replaced by the lens's index relative to that medium, so a lens weakens in water and can even diverge in a denser liquid. Power \( P=\dfrac{1}{f} \) is measured in dioptres with \( f \) in metres. For two thin lenses in contact, powers add, which means reciprocals of focal lengths add, not the focal lengths themselves. For two lenses separated by \( d \), an extra correction term must be subtracted. Keep track of signs throughout: a wrong sign on a focal length or image distance changes a real image into a virtual one and a converging system into a diverging one.
topics.worked_example: Convex lenses of focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm are 10 cm apart. \( \dfrac{1}{F}=\dfrac{1}{20}+\dfrac{1}{30}-\dfrac{10}{600}=\dfrac{4}{60} \), so \( F=15 \) cm. In contact, the same pair would give \( \dfrac{1}{F}=\dfrac{5}{60} \), \( F=12 \) cm, never \( 20+30=50 \) cm.
common_mistakes: Adding focal lengths directly for lenses in contact
Using focal length in centimetres when computing power in dioptres
Dropping the \( -\dfrac{d}{f_1f_2} \) term for separated lenses
Using the mirror formula or mirror magnification for a lens

topics.name: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
topics.summary: In a prism of angle \( A \), the refraction angles inside obey \( r_1+r_2=A \) and the deviation satisfies \( A+\delta=i+e \). As the angle of incidence increases, the deviation first falls and then rises; at the minimum \( D_m \) the ray passes symmetrically, with \( i=e \) and \( r_1=r_2=\dfrac{A}{2} \), which gives the prism formula for \( \mu \). A thin prism deviates light by \( (\mu-1)A \). When the angle at the second face exceeds the critical angle, the ray is totally reflected, and if \( A\gt2C \) no ray can emerge at all. Because \( \mu \) depends on wavelength, being largest for violet, white light is dispersed into a spectrum; dispersive power compares the angular spread with the mean deviation. Scattering by molecules is much stronger for short wavelengths (Rayleigh scattering), making the sky blue and the rising or setting Sun red, while large cloud droplets scatter all colours equally and look white. On the airless Moon, with nothing to scatter sunlight, the daytime sky looks black.
topics.worked_example: A prism with \( A=60^\circ \) has \( \mu=\sqrt{2} \). At minimum deviation, \( \sin\left(\frac{60^\circ+D_m}{2}\right)=\sqrt{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \), so the half-angle is \( 45^\circ \) and \( D_m=30^\circ \); the angle of incidence is \( 45^\circ \).
common_mistakes: Using the full angles instead of half angles in the prism formula
Multiplying by \( \mu \) instead of \( (\mu-1) \) for a thin prism
Dividing by \( \mu_y \) rather than \( \mu_y-1 \) in dispersive power
Claiming red light is scattered or deviated more than blue

topics.name: Optical Instruments: Defects of Vision, Simple/Compound Microscope, and Telescope
topics.summary: A normal eye sees from about 25 cm (near point \( D \)) to infinity. Myopia (far point too close) is corrected by a concave lens that images distant objects at the far point; hypermetropia and presbyopia (near point too far) by a convex lens; astigmatism by a cylindrical lens. A simple magnifier has magnifying power \( 1+\dfrac{D}{f} \) when the image is at the near point but only \( \dfrac{D}{f} \) when it is at infinity for relaxed viewing. A compound microscope multiplies the objective's and eyepiece's magnifications; high power needs both focal lengths small. An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has magnifying power \( -\dfrac{f_o}{f_e} \) and length \( f_o+f_e \); high power needs a large objective focal length and a small eyepiece focal length, the opposite of a microscope. Reflecting telescopes avoid chromatic aberration and allow very large objectives. Unless stated, questions assume normal adjustment with the final image at infinity; any near-point variant is labelled explicitly, and corrective lens powers are always found with focal lengths in metres.
topics.worked_example: A telescope with \( f_o=100 \) cm and \( f_e=5 \) cm has \( m=-20 \) in normal adjustment and a tube 105 cm long. If the final image is instead at the near point, \( |m|=20\left(1+\dfrac{5}{25}\right)=24 \).
common_mistakes: Adding '+1' to the magnifier formula when the image is at infinity, or dropping it at the near point
Applying the telescope's large-objective rule to a microscope
Correcting myopia with a convex lens
Using focal lengths in centimetres when finding lens power

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: Using the Cartesian sign convention, which relation correctly connects the object distance \( u \), image distance \( v \) and focal length \( f \) of a spherical mirror?
questions.explanation:
For a spherical mirror, with all distances measured from the pole and the incident-light direction taken positive, the mirror formula is \( \dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \).

The minus sign version \( \dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \) belongs to thin lenses, not mirrors.
questions.hint: Mirrors add the two reciprocals; lenses subtract them.
distractor_logic: This is the thin-lens formula; borrowing the lens sign pattern for a mirror is the classic mix-up
Reverses the order of the lens-style subtraction, which matches neither the mirror nor the lens relation
Adds the distances themselves instead of their reciprocals

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. What is its focal length, with sign, in the Cartesian convention?
questions.explanation:
For a spherical mirror, \( f=\dfrac{R}{2} \), so the magnitude is 15 cm.

The focus of a concave mirror lies in front of it, against the incident-light direction, so \( f=-15 \) cm.
questions.hint: Focal length is half the radius; think about which side of the mirror the focus lies on.
distractor_logic: Gives the concave mirror a positive sign, as if it followed a converging lens's convention
Takes the focal length equal to the radius of curvature instead of half of it
Doubles the radius instead of halving it

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: In the Cartesian sign convention, what is the sign of the focal length of a convex mirror, and why?
options: Negative, because its focus is virtual
Positive only when the object lies beyond the centre of curvature
Positive, because its focus lies behind the mirror, along the direction of the incident light
Negative, because a convex mirror diverges the reflected rays
questions.explanation:
Signs depend on direction measured from the pole: along the incident light is positive.

A convex mirror's focus lies behind the reflecting surface, so its \( f \) is positive.
questions.hint: Locate the focus relative to the pole and compare with the direction of incident light.
distractor_logic: Being virtual does not decide the sign; the side on which the focus lies does
Focal length is a property of the mirror and does not depend on where the object is placed
Assigns a sign from the diverging behaviour, the way a concave lens is treated, instead of from the position of the focus

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: An object is placed 12 cm in front of a plane mirror. What is the distance between the object and its image?
questions.explanation:
A plane mirror forms the image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

Image is 12 cm behind, object 12 cm in front, so the separation is \( 12+12=24 \) cm.
questions.hint: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
distractor_logic: That is only the image's distance from the mirror, not from the object
Halves the object distance, as if the image formed midway
Assumes the image forms on the mirror surface itself

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: What is the expression for the linear magnification \( m \) produced by a spherical mirror in the Cartesian sign convention?
questions.explanation:
For a mirror, \( m=\dfrac{h'}{h}=-\dfrac{v}{u} \).

The lens relation \( m=\dfrac{v}{u} \) has no minus sign, which is why the two must not be swapped.
questions.hint: The mirror magnification carries a minus sign that the lens version does not.
distractor_logic: This is the lens magnification; the mirror version carries a minus sign
Inverts the ratio of image and object distances
Inverts the ratio and also drops the mirror's minus sign

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: For a real object, what kind of image does a convex mirror always form?
options: Real, erect and of the same size
questions.explanation:
Rays reflected from a convex mirror always diverge, so they only appear to meet behind the mirror.

The image is therefore virtual, erect and smaller than the object, for every object position.
questions.hint: Reflected rays from a convex mirror never actually meet.
distractor_logic: This describes a concave mirror with the object beyond the centre of curvature
This is a concave mirror with the object between the pole and the focus
No mirror forms a real erect image of a real object

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Where does the image form, and what is its nature?
options: \( v=+30 \) cm; virtual, erect and of the same size
\( v=-15 \) cm; real, at the focus
\( v=-30 \) cm; real, inverted and of the same size
questions.explanation:
Here \( u=-30 \) cm and \( f=-15 \) cm.

\( \dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{f}-\dfrac{1}{u}=-\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{30}=-\dfrac{1}{30} \), so \( v=-30 \) cm.

\( m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=-1 \): real, inverted, same size, at the centre of curvature.
questions.hint: The centre of curvature is at twice the focal length.
distractor_logic: Sign slip: a positive image distance puts the image behind the mirror
An image at the focus arises only for an object at infinity
An image at infinity arises only when the object is at the focus

questions.topic: Reflection at Plane and Spherical Mirrors: Mirror Formula and Magnification
questions.question: A mirror forms an image with magnification \( m=-2 \). What does this tell you about the image?
options: It is virtual, erect and twice the size of the object
It is real, inverted and half the size of the object
It is virtual, inverted and twice the size of the object
It is real, inverted and twice the size of the object
questions.explanation:
The sign of \( m \) gives orientation: negative means inverted.

\( |m|=2 \) means the image is twice as tall; an inverted image from a mirror with a real object is real.
questions.hint: Sign tells orientation; magnitude tells size.
distractor_logic: A negative \( m \) means inverted, not erect
Reads the size factor as the reciprocal of \( |m| \)
For a single mirror and a real object, an inverted image is always real, not virtual

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: The refractive index of glass is \( \mu=1.5 \). Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, what is the speed of light in glass?
questions.explanation:
\( \mu=\dfrac{c}{v} \), so \( v=\dfrac{c}{\mu}=\dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{1.5}=2\times10^{8} \) m/s.

Since \( \mu\gt1 \), light always travels slower in the medium.
questions.hint: Refractive index is the ratio of speed in vacuum to speed in the medium.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by the refractive index, so light would speed up in a denser medium, which never happens
Assumes light keeps its vacuum speed inside glass
Divides \( c \) by 2 instead of by \( \mu \)

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: Which pair of conditions is required for total internal reflection?
options: Light goes from a rarer to a denser medium, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
Light goes from a denser to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
Light goes from a denser to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle
Light may go in either direction, provided the angle of incidence is \( 90^\circ \)
questions.explanation:
TIR needs the refracted ray to bend away from the normal, which only happens going from denser to rarer.

It also needs the angle of incidence to exceed the critical angle \( C \).
questions.hint: Which way must light bend at the boundary for the refracted ray to disappear?
distractor_logic: Going into a denser medium bends light toward the normal, so it can always refract; TIR is impossible
Below the critical angle the ray still refracts out
Direction matters: TIR never happens when entering a denser medium

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: A medium has refractive index \( \mu \) relative to air. Which expression gives its critical angle \( C \)?
questions.explanation:
At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface: \( \mu\sin C=1\times\sin 90^\circ \).

So \( \sin C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \).
questions.hint: Apply Snell's law with the refracted angle equal to a right angle.
distractor_logic: Treats the ratio as the angle itself instead of its sine
Inverts the ratio; since \( \mu\gt1 \), a sine greater than 1 is impossible
Uses cosine instead of sine

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: A transparent medium has \( \mu=2 \). What is its critical angle with air?
questions.explanation:
\( \sin C=\dfrac{1}{\mu}=\dfrac{1}{2} \).

So \( C=30^\circ \).
questions.hint: Find the angle whose sine equals \( \dfrac{1}{\mu} \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \) directly, treating the ratio as an angle
Uses \( \cos C=\dfrac{1}{\mu} \)
This is the critical angle for \( \mu=\sqrt{2} \)

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: A ray in air strikes a glass surface (\( \mu=\sqrt{3} \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 60^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation:
\( 1\times\sin 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}\sin r \).

\( \sin r=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( r=30^\circ \).
questions.hint: Use \( \mu_1\sin i=\mu_2\sin r \).
distractor_logic: Assumes the ray passes into glass without bending
Guesses a standard angle without applying Snell's law
A ray entering a denser medium bends toward the normal, never to a right angle

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: A coin lies at the bottom of a tank of water 12 cm deep (\( \mu=\dfrac{4}{3} \)). Viewed from directly above, how deep does it appear?
questions.explanation:
Apparent depth \( =\dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\mu}=\dfrac{12}{4/3} \).

This gives 9 cm, so the coin appears raised by 3 cm.
questions.hint: Objects under water look shallower than they really are.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by the refractive index; the coin appears raised, not lowered
Ignores refraction at the water surface
Gives the upward shift instead of the apparent depth

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: A ray passes obliquely from water into air. How does it bend?
questions.explanation:
Water is denser than air, so light speeds up on entering air.

Going from denser to rarer, the ray bends away from the normal.
questions.hint: Is light entering a faster or slower medium?
distractor_logic: Bending toward the normal happens when light enters a denser medium
An oblique ray changes direction whenever the refractive index changes
TIR occurs only when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle

questions.topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection, and Refraction at a Spherical Surface
questions.question: On what principle does an optical fibre carry light along its length?
options: Repeated refraction from a rarer core into a denser cladding
Scattering of light by the glass molecules
Dispersion of light into its colours
Repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the denser core and rarer cladding
questions.explanation:
The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding.

Light hitting the core-cladding boundary above the critical angle is totally reflected again and again.
questions.hint: The light must be trapped inside the core.
distractor_logic: The core is the denser medium; light going into a denser cladding could not undergo TIR
Scattering would spread and lose light, not guide it
Dispersion separates colours; it does not trap light

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: Using the Cartesian sign convention, which is the thin-lens formula?
questions.explanation:
For thin lenses, with distances from the optical centre and incident light positive: \( \dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \).

The mirror formula adds the reciprocals, so the two must not be interchanged.
questions.hint: Lenses subtract; mirrors add.
distractor_logic: This is the mirror formula; the lens relation subtracts the reciprocals
Reverses the subtraction, which flips the sign of every focal length
An invented form mixing the mirror sum with a sign flip

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: A convex lens has focal length 50 cm. What is its power?
questions.explanation:
\( P=\dfrac{1}{f} \) with \( f \) in metres: \( f=+0.5 \) m.

\( P=\dfrac{1}{0.5}=+2 \) D.
questions.hint: Convert to metres before taking the reciprocal.
distractor_logic: Uses the focal length in centimetres instead of metres
A converging lens has positive focal length and positive power
Takes power equal to the focal length in metres rather than its reciprocal

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: In the Cartesian sign convention, what is the sign of the focal length of a concave lens?
options: Positive, because concave lenses converge light
Negative only when the object lies inside the focal length
Negative, because it is a diverging lens whose focus lies on the incident side
It depends on which side of the lens the object is placed
questions.explanation:
A concave lens spreads parallel rays so they seem to come from a focus on the incident side.

That focus lies against the incident direction, so \( f \) is negative.
questions.hint: Where do parallel rays appear to diverge from?
distractor_logic: A concave lens diverges light; the converging one is convex
Focal length is fixed by the lens, not by the object position
The sign of focal length is a property of the lens alone

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: Two thin lenses of power \( +2 \) D and \( -1 \) D are placed in contact. What is the power of the combination?
questions.explanation:
For lenses in contact, powers add: \( P=P_1+P_2 \).

\( P=+2+(-1)=+1 \) D.
questions.hint: Powers of lenses in contact simply add, with signs.
distractor_logic: Ignores the negative sign of the diverging lens
Multiplies the powers instead of adding them
Averages the powers instead of adding them

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: What is the expression for the linear magnification of a thin lens in the Cartesian convention?
questions.explanation:
For a lens, \( m=\dfrac{h'}{h}=\dfrac{v}{u} \).

The minus sign appears only in the mirror version \( m=-\dfrac{v}{u} \).
questions.hint: The lens magnification has no minus sign.
distractor_logic: This is the mirror magnification, which has a minus sign
Inverts the ratio
Inverts the ratio and adds the mirror's minus sign

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Describe the image.
options: \( v=-20 \) cm; virtual, erect, same size
\( v=+20 \) cm; real, inverted, same size
\( v=+10 \) cm; real, at the focus
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{f}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{20}=\dfrac{1}{20} \), so \( v=+20 \) cm.

\( m=\dfrac{v}{u}=-1 \): real, inverted, same size, at \( 2F \).
questions.hint: The object is at twice the focal length.
distractor_logic: Sign slip that places the image on the object side
An image at the focus arises only for an object at infinity
An image at infinity arises only for an object at the focus

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: On which quantities does the focal length of a thin lens in air depend, according to the lens maker's formula?
options: Only the radii of curvature of the surfaces
The refractive index of the lens material and the radii of curvature of its two surfaces
Only the thickness of the lens at its centre
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) \).

So \( f \) depends on the material through \( \mu \) and on the shape through \( R_1 \) and \( R_2 \).
questions.hint: Recall the lens maker's formula.
distractor_logic: Focal length is a property of the lens and does not change with the object
Leaves out the \( (\mu-1) \) factor from the material
Thin-lens theory neglects thickness; material and curvature decide focal length

questions.topic: Thin Lenses: Lens Maker's Formula, Lens Formula, Power, and Combination of Lenses
questions.question: One dioptre is equal to which of these?
questions.explanation:
Power \( P=\dfrac{1}{f} \) with \( f \) in metres.

A lens of focal length 1 m has power 1 D, so \( 1 \) D \( =1\,\text{m}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Power is one over focal length in metres.
distractor_logic: Uses centimetres; the dioptre is defined with metres
Power is the reciprocal of a length, not a length
Confuses \( 1\,\text{cm}^{-1} \) with the dioptre

questions.topic: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
questions.question: For refraction through a prism of angle \( A \), with angle of incidence \( i \), angle of emergence \( e \) and deviation \( \delta \), which relation holds?
questions.explanation:
Deviation \( \delta=(i-r_1)+(e-r_2) \) and \( r_1+r_2=A \).

So \( \delta=i+e-A \), i.e. \( A+\delta=i+e \).
questions.hint: Deviation is the sum of the bending at the two faces.
distractor_logic: Puts the deviation on the wrong side of the relation
Adds all angles together without geometric basis
Subtracts the deviation instead of adding it

questions.topic: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
questions.question: Inside a prism of angle \( A \), the refraction angles at the two faces are \( r_1 \) and \( r_2 \). What is their relation?
questions.explanation:
The normals at the two faces meet at an angle of \( 180^\circ-A \).

In the triangle formed with the ray inside, \( r_1+r_2+(180^\circ-A)=180^\circ \), so \( r_1+r_2=A \).
questions.hint: Look at the triangle formed by the two normals and the ray inside the prism.
distractor_logic: Confuses the internal angles with the deviation
Uses a difference instead of a sum
Confuses the angle between the two face normals with the sum of the refraction angles

questions.topic: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
questions.question: At the position of minimum deviation through a prism, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence.

Then \( r_1=r_2 \), and since \( r_1+r_2=A \), each is \( \dfrac{A}{2} \).
questions.hint: The ray passes symmetrically through the prism.
distractor_logic: The two angles add up to \( A \), so each cannot equal \( A \)
Confuses the internal refraction angles with half the deviation
Describes normal incidence, which is not the minimum deviation setting

questions.topic: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
questions.question: Which formula gives the refractive index \( \mu \) of a prism of angle \( A \) and minimum deviation \( D_m \)?
questions.explanation:
At minimum deviation \( i=\dfrac{A+D_m}{2} \) and \( r=\dfrac{A}{2} \).

Snell's law \( \mu=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} \) gives the prism formula.
questions.hint: Combine Snell's law with the symmetric-passage angles.
distractor_logic: Inverted ratio, which would give \( \mu\lt1 \)
Uses the full angles instead of the half angles
Subtracts the deviation instead of adding it

questions.topic: Refraction Through a Prism, Dispersion, and Scattering of Light
questions.question: Why does the clear daytime sky look blue?
options: Air molecules scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones
Air molecules scatter red light much more strongly than blue
Light reflected from the oceans colours the sky
Raindrops disperse sunlight into its colours overhead
questions.explanation:
Rayleigh scattering by molecules is proportional to \( \dfrac{1}{\lambda^{4}} \).

Blue light, with its shorter wavelength, is scattered across the sky much more than red.

questions.question: Why does an air bubble in water behave like a diverging lens, even though it is convex in shape?

Only concave shapes can diverge light

A convex shape with a negative factor gives a negative focal length: a diverging lens.
